questions.question: What is Enumerable and what are its common methods?
questions.title: Ruby Enumerable
questions.direct_answer: Enumerable is a module mixed into Array and Hash (and others) that gives you a large set of iteration methods: each (iterate), map (transform to a new array), select (keep matching), reject (drop matching), reduce (fold to one value), find (first match), sort, group_by, flat_map. You include Enumerable in your own class and define each, and you get all of them for free. They're the heart of Ruby's collection-processing style — short, expressive chains that replace most loops.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Enumerable is a module mixed into Array/Hash and can name map/select/reduce/each and that they're free once you define each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using each when map/select/reduce express the intent better, or not knowing reduce's accumulator.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Enumerable is a module mixed into Array/Hash giving each/map/select/reject/reduce/find/sort. Include it + define each to get them all in your own class.

sections.title: The Iteration Toolkit
sections.content: Enumerable is a module mixed into Array and Hash, and others, that gives you a large set of iteration methods: each to iterate, map to transform to a new array, select to keep matching, reject to drop matching, reduce to fold to a single value, find to return the first match, sort, group_by, and flat_map. You include Enumerable in your own class and define each, and you get all of them for free. They're the heart of Ruby's collection-processing style — short, expressive chains like arr.map { ... }.select { ... }.reduce(0, :+) that replace most explicit loops and read like a pipeline of what you want, not how to loop.

sections.title: Enumerable Methods
sections.content:
each/map/select/reduce and more — free once you define each.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[class includes Enumerable] --> E[define each]
  E --> M[map/select/reduce/find/sort... all work]
```

sections.title: Common Enumerable methods
sections.content:
```ruby
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

nums.each { |n| puts n }                 # iterate (no return value used)
nums.map { |n| n * 2 }                    # [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] (transform)
nums.select { |n| n.even? }               # [2, 4] (keep matching)
nums.reject { |n| n.even? }               # [1, 3, 5] (drop matching)
nums.reduce(0) { |sum, n| sum + n }       # 15 (fold to one value)
nums.find { |n| n > 3 }                   # 4 (first match)
nums.group_by { |n| n.even? }            # {true=>[2,4], false=>[1,3,5]}
nums.flat_map { |n| [n, n * 10] }         # [1,10,2,20,3,30,4,40,5,50]

# Include in your own class — define each, get the rest:
class Deck
  include Enumerable
  def initialize; @cards = (1..52).to_a; end
  def each(&b); @cards.each(&b); end   # now map/select/sort all work
end
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using each when map/select/reduce expresses the intent better and more briefly.
Not knowing reduce's accumulator (the running value; pass the initial value).
Forgetting you get all of Enumerable by defining each in your own class.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Enumerable is a module mixed into Array/Hash with each/map/select/reject/reduce/find/sort.
Include it in your own class and define each to get all of them for free.
map transforms to a new array; select keeps matches; reduce folds to one value.
Use the method that expresses intent (map over each, select over each + if).
group_by returns a hash; flat_map flattens one level after mapping.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Enumerable is a module mixed into Array and Hash, and others, that gives you a large set of iteration methods: each to iterate, map to transform to a new array, select to keep matching, reject to drop matching, reduce to fold to a single value, find to return the first match, sort, group_by, and flat_map. You include Enumerable in your own class and define each, and you get all of them for free. They're the heart of Ruby's collection-processing style — short, expressive chains like map then select then reduce that replace most explicit loops and read like a pipeline of what you want, not how to loop. A common mistake is using each when map or select or reduce expresses the intent better and more briefly, and not knowing reduce's accumulator, the running value, where you pass the initial value.
